questions.question: A fixed benefit $B>0$ is paid at the death time $T_x$ of a life alive at age $x$. Assume $T_x$ has a nondegenerate continuous law and force of interest $\delta>0$. Why can the present value vary even though $B$ is fixed?
options: Only randomness in the benefit amount can change its present value.
The current age alone determines the realised discount factor.
The expected death time is selected as the actual payment date.
The random death time changes the discount applied to the benefit.

questions.question: An insurance cash flow has integrable random present value $Z$. On a fixed mortality and interest basis, what does its actuarial present value $\mathbb{E}[Z]$ describe?
options: The amount Z realised for whichever outcome eventually occurs.
A deterministic probability-weighted average of possible present values.
The largest discounted value attainable under the mortality model.
The nominal benefit before applying any interest discount factor.

questions.question: A benefit $B>0$ is payable at time $t>0$ only if the insured life survives to that time. The annual discount factor is $v>0$. What present value does this particular benefit contribute on an outcome where the life dies before $t$?
options: Zero, because the contractual payment condition fails.
B, because the amount of the promised benefit is fixed.
B times v to the power t, because every benefit is discounted.
B times the death probability, because the insured dies first.

questions.question: Annual effective interest $i$ gives annual discount factor $v=(1+i)^{-1}$. Which condition on $i$ is necessary and sufficient for $v$ to be positive and finite on this actuarial present-value basis?

An annual discount factor $0<v<1$ and a constant force of interest $\delta$ describe the same basis, so a payment at time $t\ge0$ is discounted both by $v^t$ and by $\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}$. Which relation must hold?
options: $\delta=-\log v$.
$\delta=\log v$.
$\delta=1-v$.

questions.question: A benefit of 100 is payable at time 2 only on survival. For a life currently alive, that survival probability is 0.8, and the annual discount factor is $v=0.9$. What is its actuarial present value?

A life has almost surely finite future lifetime $T_x>0$. At death a benefit $b(T_x)=\mathrm{e}^{\delta T_x}$ is paid, under the same constant force of interest $\delta>0$. What is its actuarial present value?
options: $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\delta T_x}]$.
$\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-\delta T_x}]$.

questions.question: An insurance cash flow has integrable present value $Z$ and actuarial present value 12. A second contract doubles every payment amount but keeps all payment dates and conditions unchanged. What is the second actuarial present value?

A life receives 10 at time 1 if alive then and 20 at time 2 if alive then. The respective survival probabilities from today are 0.8 and 0.6, and the annual discount factor is $v=0.5$. What is the total actuarial present value?
A fixed benefit of 50 is paid at the almost surely finite death time $T_x$ of a currently alive life. Annual interest is zero. What is its actuarial present value?
options: $50\mathbb{E}[T_x]$.

questions.question: A fixed death benefit $B>0$ is paid at an almost surely finite future lifetime $T_x\ge0$, with force of interest $\delta\ge0$. The mean of $T_x$ is infinite. What can be concluded about the actuarial present value?
options: It is infinite because the mean future lifetime is infinite.
It is unavailable unless the expected death time is first calculated.
It equals zero because infinite mean implies no finite payment.
It is finite because the discounted benefit is bounded by B.

questions.question: On one fixed mortality and discount basis, two non-negative death benefits satisfy $b_1(t)\le b_2(t)$ at every possible death time $t\ge0$. Both discounted benefits are integrable. Which comparison is guaranteed for every such pair of benefits?
options: $\operatorname{APV}_1\ge\operatorname{APV}_2$.
$\operatorname{APV}_1\le\operatorname{APV}_2$.
$\operatorname{APV}_1=\operatorname{APV}_2$ necessarily.
Their ordering requires the two benefit amounts to be independent.

questions.question: A fixed death benefit $B>0$ is paid at an almost surely finite future lifetime $T_x>0$, under positive force of interest $\delta>0$. Which bound on its actuarial present value holds for every such lifetime law?
options: $\operatorname{APV}\ge B$.
$\operatorname{APV}=B$ necessarily.
$0<\operatorname{APV}\le B$.
$\operatorname{APV}=0$ necessarily.

questions.question: A life has future lifetime $T_x$ uniform on $(0,1)$ years. A fixed benefit of 100 is paid at death. The force of interest is $\delta=\log 2$, so the time-$t$ discount factor is $2^{-t}$. What is its actuarial present value?
A contract pays only on an event A, with probability 0.4. Its integrable random present value $Z$ is zero otherwise, and $\mathbb{E}[Z\mid A]=30$. What is its actuarial present value?

A unit benefit is paid at future lifetime $T_x$, uniform on $(0,2)$ years. Force of interest is $\delta=\log2$, giving discount factor $2^{-t}$ at time $t$. Since $\mathbb{E}[T_x]=1$, does valuing at this mean time give the true actuarial present value?
options: Yes; both procedures give $1/2$ because the lifetime mean is one.
No; APV is the endpoint average $5/8$ rather than $1/2$.
No; averaging gives $3/(8\log2)$, while mean-time valuation gives $1/2$.
Yes; both procedures give $1$ because death eventually occurs.

questions.question: A life receives 100 at time 1 if alive then and 100 at time 2 if alive then. Under annual discount factor $v=0.8$, proposed APVs for these separate benefits are 40 and 50. Do these prices imply a coherent survival basis for the currently alive cohort?
options: No; implied two-year survival exceeds implied one-year survival.
Yes; both implied survival probabilities lie between zero and one.
Yes; deaths between dates can increase the later survival probability.
No; the time-2 benefit should use one discount factor rather than two.

questions.question: A life has future lifetime $T_x$ uniform on $(0,1)$ years. A signed cash flow $b(t)=\mathrm{e}^{\delta t}/(t-1/2)$ is paid at death under force of interest $\delta>0$. The value at $t=1/2$ may be assigned arbitrarily. Does symmetric cancellation around $1/2$ establish an actuarial present value of zero?
options: Yes; symmetric positive and negative terms always define a mean.
Yes; the singular death time has probability zero and can be removed.
No; APV is $+\infty$, since the positive expected part diverges.
No; the positive and negative expected parts are both infinite.
